learn.title: Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV)
learn.intro: Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV) transforms solar panels into architectural elements like roofs and facades, merging clean energy with urban design. This innovation reduces construction costs, enhances energy efficiency, and supports global decarbonization goals by generating power on-site.
learn.c1_text: BIPV replaces traditional building materials with solar cells, such as solar roofs or windows. Like a house's roof generating electricity while shielding from weather, BIPV integrates seamlessly into structures. Over 30% of new buildings in Europe now include BIPV systems, cutting energy bills by up to 20%.
learn.c2_text: Modern BIPV systems achieve 15-22% efficiency, comparable to rooftop panels but with added value from eliminating separate materials. For example, a 10 kW BIPV system can save $15,000 in roofing costs while generating $1,200 annually in energy. Thin-film BIPV also improves building insulation.
learn.c3_text: India's Ministry of New and Renewable Energy promotes BIPV under its National Solar Mission. Projects like the 1.5 MW BIPV installation at IIT Delhi showcase solar-integrated facades. States like Gujarat offer subsidies for solar rooftops, driving adoption in commercial and residential sectors.
learn.stat2: BIPV systems reduce building energy costs by 15-30%
learn.stat3: Europe: 40% of new buildings use BIPV (2022)

learn.title: Agrivoltaics: Solar + Farming
learn.intro: Agrivoltaics combines solar panels with agriculture, enabling dual land use for energy and food production. This innovative approach increases land efficiency, protects crops from extreme weather, and boosts farmer incomes while advancing renewable energy goals globally.
learn.c1_text: Solar panels elevated above crops create shade that reduces water evaporation and protects plants from hail. For example, in Arizona, agrivoltaic systems increased vegetable yields by 20% while generating 1.5 MW of power. Panels are spaced to allow 80% sunlight for crops below.
learn.c2_text: Studies show agrivoltaics can produce 50% more energy than traditional solar farms while improving crop resilience. Crops like tomatoes and lettuce thrive under partial shade, with yields up to 30% higher. The system's elevated design also enables livestock grazing beneath panels.
learn.c3_text: In Andhra Pradesh, the 1 MW agrivoltaic project at Kakatiya University demonstrates solar-powered irrigation and crop cultivation. Similarly, Gujarat's 5 MW facility in Kutch combines date palms with solar arrays. The Ministry of Agriculture supports such models to enhance rural livelihoods.
learn.stat1: Agrivoltaics can increase land use efficiency by 60%
learn.stat2: Crops under panels show 15-30% higher water-use efficiency
learn.stat3: Germany: 10% of solar farms use agrivoltaic design

learn.title: Commercial Vehicle Electrification
learn.intro: Electric buses and trucks are revolutionizing urban and freight transport, cutting emissions and operational costs. As governments mandate zero-emission fleets, this shift relies on battery innovation, charging infrastructure, and policy support to transform transportation sectors globally.
learn.c1_text: Electric buses eliminate tailpipe emissions and reduce fuel costs by 70% compared to diesel. China leads with 90% of new buses electric, while cities like Delhi operate 500+ e-buses. Charging at depots overnight saves 40% in energy costs via time-of-use tariffs.
learn.c2_text: Hydrogen fuel cells and lithium-ion batteries power long-haul trucks, with Tesla's Semi targeting 500-mile ranges. The US aims for 50% of medium/heavy trucks to be zero-emission by 2030. Charging hubs along highways, like California's 1,000+ stations, enable seamless operations.
learn.c3_text: India's FAME II scheme subsidizes 100% e-bus purchases for cities. Tata Motors' 15m electric truck plant in Jamshedpur supports local manufacturing. States like Maharashtra offer tax waivers for EV freight, while startups like Olectra partner with BYD for 1,000 e-buses in Nagpur.
learn.stat2: E-buses reduce CO2 by 50% vs diesel (per mile)

learn.title: Carbon Markets and Credits
learn.intro: Carbon markets and credits incentivize clean energy by pricing emissions, driving investment in renewables and efficiency. By linking pollution costs to economic rewards, these mechanisms help nations meet climate targets while mobilizing private capital for sustainable projects globally.
learn.c1_text: Carbon credits represent 1 ton of CO2 reduced or removed. Companies buy credits to offset emissions, funding projects like wind farms. For example, a $10/ton credit in the EU ETS finances 100 MW of solar. Over 400 million tons of CO2 have been offset globally via such markets.
learn.c2_text: The Paris Agreement mandates carbon pricing, with 64 countries implementing ETS. India's Perform, Achieve, Trade (PAT) scheme has reduced industrial emissions by 5% since 2018. Voluntary markets like Gold Standard verify projects, attracting $2 billion in 2022 for reforestation and solar initiatives.
learn.c3_text: India's carbon market expanded by 20% in 2023, with 200+ industrial consumers trading credits under PAT. Renewable energy projects account for 35% of verified credits. The government plans a national ETS by 2025, targeting 100 million tons of CO2 reductions annually.
learn.stat2: India's PAT scheme reduced industrial emissions by 5%
learn.stat3: EU ETS covers 40% of EU emissions

learn.title: Sodium-Ion Batteries
learn.intro: Sodium-ion batteries offer a low-cost, abundant alternative to lithium-ion, using sodium-rich materials for grid storage. With rising demand for renewable energy storage, this technology promises to democratize access while addressing lithium supply chain vulnerabilities and material costs.
learn.c1_text: Sodium-ion batteries use sodium from seawater, avoiding lithium's scarcity. They achieve 160-200 Wh/kg energy density, 70% of lithium's but at 30% lower cost. CATL's 2023 prototype powers 100 MWh grid systems, ideal for daily storage cycles with 6,000+ lifespans.
learn.c2_text: Sodium is 1,000x more abundant than lithium, with raw material costs 50% lower. Production lines can retrofit lithium factories with minimal changes. By 2030, sodium-ion could supply 30% of EV batteries, reducing costs by $5,000 per vehicle compared to lithium-ion.
learn.c3_text: India's Department of Science developed sodium-ion tech under its National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems. Startups like SFL Energy are piloting sodium-ion batteries for 50 MW solar storage in Rajasthan. The government offers 30% subsidies for domestic production under PLI schemes.
learn.stat2: CATL's sodium-ion achieves 200 Wh/kg energy density

learn.title: Direct Air Carbon Capture
learn.intro: Direct Air Capture (DAC) removes CO2 directly from ambient air, powered by renewables to achieve negative emissions. This technology complements renewable energy by storing carbon permanently, offering a critical tool for achieving net-zero goals and mitigating climate change impacts globally.
learn.c1_text: DAC systems use fans to pull air through filters or chemical solutions that bind CO2. Climeworks' plant in Switzerland captures 4,000 tons/year, storing it underground. Powered by solar/wind, DAC requires 500 kWh per ton of CO2—equivalent to 2 hours of home electricity use.
learn.c2_text: DAC needs 1.5-2 GJ per ton of CO2, demanding renewable energy integration. By 2050, 100 DAC plants could remove 500 million tons annually—10% of global emissions. Carbon Engineering's Canadian project uses waste heat and solar to cut energy use by 40%, scaling to 1 million tons/year by 2030.
learn.c3_text: India's National Centre for Sustainable Management is testing DAC in Rajasthan's solar-rich regions. A proposed 50,000-ton/year plant near Delhi could use 100 MW solar power. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy offers $50/ton subsidies to incentivize DAC deployment in high-CO2 sectors.
learn.stat2: DAC requires 500 kWh electricity per ton of CO2
learn.stat4: DAC can remove 500 Mt CO2/year by 2050
